evidence.claim: Cached Layer 1 evidence identifies Lamb Weston as a public supplier of value-added frozen potato products, including French fries, to QSR chains, foodservice distributors, and retail channels.

Cached Layer 1 evidence maps JBT Marel to food-processing equipment and automation; if frozen fry producers need throughput, yield, consistency, or capacity additions, this equipment layer could become chokepoint-adjacent.

External context from Westrock Coffee investor material describes the company as a beverage-solutions provider supplying major brands with coffee, tea, and related products, and highlights resilient coffee demand and projected RTD coffee growth.

Cached Layer 1 evidence maps Americold to temperature-controlled warehousing and cold-chain logistics, while noting direct exposure to frozen potato processors, QSR distributors, or foodservice throughput remains an evidence gap.
Cached Layer 1 evidence maps Lineage to temperature-controlled warehousing and integrated cold-chain logistics, while noting restaurant-specific NOI/customer exposure remains an evidence gap.
Cached Layer 1 evidence identifies Sysco as a broadline foodservice distributor and reference node for restaurant procurement, private-label products, logistics, and upstream supplier access.

Cached Layer 1 evidence identifies US Foods as a distributor of fresh, frozen, dry food, and non-food products to foodservice customers, with potential relevance to private-brand SKUs and frozen/refrigerated throughput.

Cached Layer 1 evidence maps Performance Food Group to foodservice distribution and proprietary/private-label exposure, making it a second-order restaurant case-volume and procurement-consolidation node.

External context on Kura Sushi USA indicates restaurant procurement concentration can be a material issue for small-cap restaurant operators when food-and-beverage purchases are concentrated among specialized distributors; this supports the broader GENK diligence lens by analogy, not as company-specific evidence.

memory_update.content: For the Restaurants theme, direct upstream restaurant input suppliers with measurable customer, capacity, and margin signals should outrank highly followed restaurant brands and broad distributors unless distributors provide unique evidence on case volumes or procurement consolidation.

LW is the highest-priority candidate in this chunk because it combines direct restaurant input exposure, public-market purity, evidence quality, bottleneck plausibility, and falsifiable customer/volume/margin signals.

JBTM and WEST should remain on the underfollowed watchlist. JBTM requires order/backlog proof from food and potato processors. WEST requires customer concentration, foodservice mix, leverage, commodity pass-through, and cash-flow verification before promotion beyond speculative shadow.

SYY, USFD, and PFGC are useful evidence nodes for restaurant demand, private-label penetration, and procurement consolidation, but their broad business mix lowers chokepoint purity and underfollowed discovery scores.

COLD and LINE have plausible restaurant cold-chain infrastructure exposure, but must show direct links to frozen potato processors, QSR distributors, foodservice customers, or restaurant-sensitive throughput before they can rank above direct input or equipment suppliers.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Whether recent volume pressure, customer exits, restructuring, ERP/service issues, or margin weakness are cyclical/self-inflicted versus evidence of lost strategic supplier status with large QSR customers.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need current primary-source confirmation of named customer exposure, contract durability, customer exits, service-level recovery, and whether any QSR share loss is structural.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Directly maps to a core restaurant/QSR input: frozen potato products and French fries. The thesis is highly testable through volume, price/mix, customer concentration, plant utilization, restructuring, ERP/service-level recovery, margin, and crop-cost disclosures. It has stronger public-market purity than distributors or REITs because the restaurant input itself is the business rather than one buried line item.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Often screened as packaged food or commodity processing rather than restaurant infrastructure. This can cause the market to miss supplier switching friction, QSR menu consistency, plant throughput, crop procurement, and customer concentration.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Order backlog or book-to-bill from potato processors, installed-base service revenue, replacement-cycle demand, and whether major frozen potato capacity additions require JBTM systems.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need segment-level evidence that potato/frozen-food processors are material customers and that incremental restaurant/frozen-fry demand is visible in orders, backlog, or service revenue.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Second-order equipment node with potential leverage to frozen-food capacity, potato processing lines, industrial frying, freezing/chilling, yield improvement, and automation. If processors need better throughput or consistency, equipment suppliers may become chokepoint-adjacent even though they are not restaurant brands.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Usually classified as industrial machinery or food-tech rather than a restaurant supply-chain beneficiary. Restaurant screens may miss its relevance to fry-plant capacity, quality consistency, labor substitution, and installed-base service revenue.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Customer concentration, restaurant/foodservice revenue mix, profitability path, debt maturity schedule, commodity pass-through mechanics, and whether new capacity can generate durable margins.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need audited revenue mix by foodservice/restaurant channel, customer concentration, contract structure, coffee commodity pass-through, leverage profile, and cash-flow conversion.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Small-cap B2B coffee, tea, extracts, and private-label beverage platform with a plausible hidden restaurant/foodservice supply-chain role. External context indicates the company positions itself as a beverage-solutions provider to major brands and highlights structurally resilient global coffee demand and RTD coffee growth. This creates a testable but still speculative restaurant-adjacent thesis.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: It is not a consumer-facing restaurant brand and may be screened as a small beverage/coffee supplier. Its role can be hidden behind restaurant, retail, or consumer-brand customers that own the front-end relationship.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Direct exposure to frozen potato processors, foodservice distributors, or QSR supply chains; occupancy/throughput sensitivity to restaurant volumes; contract duration and inflation pass-through terms.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need customer/channel disclosure tying Americold facilities to frozen potato processors, QSR distributors, or restaurant foodservice demand rather than broad grocery/CPG cold storage.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Cold-chain infrastructure is necessary for frozen fries and perishable restaurant inputs. The public-market mapping is plausible and underfollowed because the company is typically viewed as a REIT rather than restaurant supply-chain infrastructure. However, restaurant-specific exposure remains insufficiently proven.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: REIT classification can obscure operational sensitivity to foodservice frozen-product throughput, temperature-controlled storage scarcity, and production-adjacent logistics needs.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Whether Sysco, US Foods, or related-party vendor purchases materially affect food costs, availability, gross margin volatility, and governance risk as the company expands.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need primary filings to quantify vendor concentration, related-party procurement, unit-level food costs, new-unit economics, and geographic expansion execution.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Small-cap restaurant operator where supply-chain structure, vendor concentration, food-cost sensitivity, and governance/related-party procurement can matter more than generic same-store-sales narratives. Public-market purity is high because it is a direct restaurant operator, but the chokepoint angle is more company-specific than industry-wide.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Small restaurant operators are less covered than national chains, and procurement details may be overlooked. Supplier concentration and related-party purchasing can create hidden operational risk or hidden margin upside if managed well.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Named or implied relationships with frozen potato processors, QSR distributors, or large foodservice customers; share of NOI from foodservice versus retail/CPG; utilization of port-oriented and production-adjacent facilities.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need disclosed customer/channel mix and facility-level exposure to foodservice, QSR, frozen potato, or restaurant distribution networks.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Large temperature-controlled warehousing and integrated cold-chain logistics platform with plausible exposure to frozen and perishable foodservice continuity. The thesis is useful as a supply-chain infrastructure mapping but needs more proof of restaurant-specific NOI or throughput sensitivity.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Although post-IPO attention exists, it may be viewed through a REIT/real-estate lens rather than as an operating chokepoint for frozen food logistics and restaurant input continuity.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Whether frozen potato/fry SKUs are meaningful within Foodservice, whether proprietary Performance Brands include fries or potato products, and whether chain-restaurant contracts create volume stickiness.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need SKU/category exposure for frozen potato products, proprietary brands, chain-restaurant contracts, and gross-margin contribution by segment.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Foodservice distribution gives direct evidence on restaurant case volumes, independent versus chain demand, frozen-food throughput, and proprietary/private-label penetration. It is useful for triangulating demand, though it is less pure and less scarce than a specialized input supplier.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Restaurant investors may focus on brand traffic and same-store sales while PFGC sits one step upstream as a logistics, availability, and private-label product layer.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Private-brand frozen potato offerings, supplier concentration with frozen potato vendors, regional fill-rate performance, and customer commitments with chain restaurants.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need evidence that frozen potato/private-brand restaurant categories are material enough to influence company-level economics.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Broadline distributor with restaurant procurement and frozen/refrigerated throughput relevance. It can serve as a demand and fill-rate evidence source, but the restaurant chokepoint thesis is diluted by broad product and customer mix.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Like other distributors, it can be missed by restaurant-brand screens even though it may carry important private-brand and regional availability signals.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Case-volume trends by independent versus chain restaurants, private-label penetration, supplier concentration, gross-margin pass-through, and whether restaurant operators are consolidating procurement toward Sysco.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need more granular category-level and supplier-level evidence to connect Sysco economics specifically to frozen fries, oils, sauces, and other restaurant input bottlenecks.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Included mainly as a reference leader and distribution gatekeeper. Sysco is a high-quality source for case-volume trends, independent versus chain restaurant demand, private-label penetration, supplier pass-through, and procurement consolidation. It is not the best underfollowed candidate because it is large, well-covered, and diversified.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Not truly underfollowed. Its value in this funnel is as an evidence node because many private or niche suppliers sell through large distributors, making Sysco useful for reading upstream restaurant input demand.

summary: Layer 3 ranking of the provided Restaurants candidate chunk prioritizes public-market mappings that sit upstream of restaurant traffic: frozen potato inputs, food-processing automation, B2B beverages, and temperature-controlled logistics. Highest priority goes to candidates with a concrete restaurant supply-chain role, testable hidden signals, and underfollowed discovery value rather than brand popularity. Lamb Weston ranks first because it is a direct QSR/menu-input supplier with unusually clear chokepoint, customer-concentration, margin, crop, and service-level questions. JBT Marel ranks second as a second-order equipment/automation node that could benefit if frozen-food and potato processors need throughput, yield, and plant-utilization improvements. Westrock Coffee ranks third as a speculative small-cap beverage-supply platform with high hidden-signal potential but weaker evidence and financial-risk clarity. Sysco is retained as a reference leader and evidence source, not an underfollowed alpha candidate.
